title: One shared hand on a fixed inclined lift
version_label: DCMP/Worlds rebuild as recalled by Jack Sarratt; exact installation dates unaudited

premises.text: Fixed approximately 30–45 degree four-stage elevator; shared cone/cube hand on a wrist; ground pickup and placement use that hand. Stage-count convention and angle reference remain unmeasured.
Later IRI interview describes a compact continuously rigged elevator and shared intake. It supports the family, not exact DCMP hardware identity.

piece_flow: Owner-described direct path: ground piece → roller hand → retained in that hand while wrist and carriage move → scoring release. Zero intermediate handoff on this described main path. Roller rotation is still a powered function; eliminating a handoff does not eliminate acquisition control.
packaging: An inclined mast occupies a fixed diagonal corridor above the chassis. The carriage carries the wrist and hand along that corridor. The wrist swings the mouth toward the floor and then to a travel or placing orientation. The hand, held piece and any protruding cone sweep beyond the carriage; their clearance must be checked at every lift position. Mast feet must react overturning loads into the chassis. Battery access, exact mounting coordinates and measured extension envelope are not established.
independent_motions: Conditional kinematic model: one coordinated lift coordinate plus wrist rotation; roller spin handles piece transport. Four stages are not automatically four independently controlled degrees of freedom. Count drive translation/yaw separately and do not infer motor count from stages. Coupling/rigging details of the recalled configuration are unknown.
burdens_avoided: The shared hand avoids transferring possession between a dedicated ground collector and scoring device on this path. A fixed mast avoids a powered shoulder angle. Fewer pose combinations can reduce collision planning and calibration work.
burdens_retained: The driver must place the shared mouth close enough to the piece. Carriage stroke couples vertical height and horizontal reach. Mast compliance, stage friction, roller contact, cone orientation, wrist holding torque, loaded CG and driver alignment remain real costs. Low independent motion count does not establish easy fabrication or a light complete robot.
engineering_hypothesis: If the task poses lie near the fixed mast trajectory and wrist reach, the architecture can obtain needed capability with fewer independent coordinates. Keeping possession in one hand removes an interface where timing, compression and support must otherwise agree. This is a plausible engineering mechanism, not a measured explanation of the season result.
rival_explanation: Driver practice, autonomous execution, matchups, alliance partners and service quality can explain high results without proving architectural superiority. A more articulated robot might recover from more pickup orientations or reach a scoring pose with less chassis repositioning.
reversal_conditions: The advantage reverses if floor capture requires slow precise alignment, mast/chassis positioning costs more time than a reliable handoff, or reach/stow/charge-station envelopes force bad routes. A wider collector can be worthwhile if acquisition dominates complete cycles.
unknowns: Exact angle, stage nomenclature, stroke, mass distribution, cone pickup orientations, handoff alternatives, battery route and dated cubeapult installation. The owner vision counterfactual and top-15–25 ranking are opinions, not predicted outcomes.
decision_changing_check: First overlay required pickup, transit and scoring poses on a side-view layout. Then compare the distribution of approach-to-secure times and complete-cycle times against a wide-collector alternative, including failed pickups. Do not build both full robots to answer a geometry question.
outcome_status: No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.
owner_attribution: Jack Sarratt supplied the geometry and direct-path account; the account is preserved rather than promoted to an independently measured specification.

title: A small extra mechanism with a specific autonomous job
version_label: IRI interview published July 2023; not backdated to DCMP

premises.text: Team describes thinner 1-inch elevator tubing to reduce high-mounted weight, custom bearing blocks and a continuously rigged belt.
Shared intake draws on 111, with a separately inspired wrist. Team discusses practice and wrist tuning.
A servo-released over-center cube launcher avoids an initial autonomous turn; high/low targets depend on routine. Exact accuracy was not measured in this review.

piece_flow: The normal shared-hand path remains separate from the launcher path. For the described autonomous feature a human preloads a cube on the launcher; release sends it rearward, allowing the robot to continue its route. Do not draw an invented automatic handoff from the roller hand into the launcher.
packaging: Reserve a rearward launch corridor, the cocked linkage envelope and safe preload access. This is a second scoring path occupying frame space even though it does not require another continuously positioned arm. Exact location, energy storage, latch loads and full return procedure are not reconstructed from captions.
independent_motions: Lift, wrist and rollers serve the main path; a servo triggers the auxiliary launcher. A binary release adds a control state and hardware even if it adds no continuously controlled positioning axis. Do not call the whole robot a two-motor mechanism.
burdens_avoided: A dedicated preloaded release can avoid spending drivetrain time on a turn. It also avoids requiring the main hand to execute that first rearward scoring operation.
burdens_retained: Preload orientation, latch repeatability, launch dispersion, game legality, reset effort and autonomous start alignment now matter. A short mechanism can create a large reliability cost if it needs delicate setup. Interview tuning/practice comments contradict any claim that simple hardware needs no integration work.
engineering_hypothesis: The relevant question is marginal autonomous score per occupied space, setup time and failure exposure. A small additional mechanism can strengthen a simple architecture when it removes a specific route penalty and leaves the ordinary cycle path uncomplicated.
rival_explanation: An improved start pose, different route or more accurate chassis control might recover the same time without the launcher. Interview success reports are not a comparison against those alternatives.
reversal_conditions: Remove or redesign it if the autonomous gain disappears under legal starts, its preload disrupts setup, it blocks service, or miss cost outweighs the extra piece. Retain useful complexity when measured gain survives these conditions.
unknowns: Installation chronology, stored-energy details, exact repeatability and whether a three-piece routine was consistently achieved. Captions are automatic and can misrecognize names/numerals; no continuous video or CAD review is claimed.
decision_changing_check: Compare legal autonomous route budgets with and without the initial turn using existing path/layout tools; only if this changes the choice, test a small launcher for dispersion and preload sensitivity.
outcome_status: No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

title: Low service burden can require careful construction
version_label: Tsunami interview plus June 29 elevator construction write-up; not one certified event configuration

premises.text: Team packages motors inline with the mast base, uses a continuous belt with few redirects and bearing-supported idlers, and adds constant-force return springs.
Team explicitly describes precision-intensive upfront assembly and reports essentially no maintenance after completion.
Existing source study records a shared claw, later wide cube collector, elevator and virtual four-bar, plus automated alignment.

piece_flow: Shared-claw path: piece enters the claw and stays with it for placement. Later cube-collector path: cube enters wide collector → crosses an additional transfer through the elevator opening → reaches the scoring claw. Keep those paths distinct; the later robot is not a universal zero-handoff example.
packaging: Elevator rails and moving stages establish the lift corridor; the end-effector linkage occupies additional swept space near the carriage. The through-opening used by the later cube path is a functional packaging feature. Inline base drive placement preserves mast overlap/travel. Belt redirects, tensioning access and return assistance must fit within the same package. Exact battery extraction and collector-to-claw contact geometry remain unresolved.
independent_motions: Lift extension plus end-effector linkage position are distinct functional coordinates; additional acquisition deployment may belong to the later collector. Link count and virtual-link geometry do not establish the number of independent axes. The drivetrain and automation are part of the complete system cost.
burdens_avoided: Compact rigging can avoid consuming mast travel with bulky base gearing. Careful belt routing can avoid friction that would otherwise demand repeated adjustment. The original shared-claw path avoids a handoff; the later path deliberately spends complexity on acquisition.
burdens_retained: Belt stiffness, alignment, bearing wear, tension setting, return consistency and precise assembly remain burdens. The team report separates low operating maintenance from manufacturing simplicity. Twelve-motor swerve and advanced alignment controls in the retained source study prevent using Tsunami as proof that every subsystem was minimal.
engineering_hypothesis: Spend fabrication effort where it produces repeatable motion and reduces event service, while evaluating the full robot on acquisition and scoring. A later wide collector is justified only by a complete-cycle benefit that outweighs its transfer and space costs.
rival_explanation: The maintenance report may reflect excellent execution, spares or operating conditions rather than a universally forgiving transmission. Fast placement may depend heavily on drivetrain control and driver workflow.
reversal_conditions: A simpler rigging method may be better if assembly capability, belt quality or alignment control cannot reproduce this construction. A wide collector can be worse if transfer jams dominate the time it saves at acquisition.
unknowns: Measured service hours, comparable elevator failure rates, exact collector handoff and verified installation chronology. No CAD release was reviewed. Do not copy nonstandard pulley bend radii from informal feel tests as validated practice.
decision_changing_check: Use a full-stroke clearance and return-force calculation first. If rigging choice remains consequential, test one representative loaded stage path and return consistency, including tolerances and service access; measure complete pickup cycles before adding a collector.
outcome_status: No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

title: What an articulated arm and a handoff actually cost
version_label: February controls write-up, May wiring report and pinned repository snapshot; event binary unverified

premises.text: Shoulder, elbow and wrist provide multiple positioning coordinates. Team describes coupled dynamics, optimized collision-constrained paths and intake avoidance.
IntakeCubeHandoff runs intake and gripper while moving the arm to CUBE_HANDOFF, then requests HOMED on termination. This verifies coordination logic, not successful physical transfer.
Team moved wiring outside the arm to ease tube replacement, accepting exposure with protective wrapping; it reports a short repair list despite electrical complexity.

piece_flow: For the inspected cube-handoff command: ground cube → dedicated cube intake → overlap with gripper at an arm handoff pose → arm-carried cube → scoring release. The command coordinates intake, arm and gripper; it does not by itself prove compression, transfer sensor coverage, success rate or the full cone route.
packaging: The arm base must carry shoulder reactions; the elbow and wrist sweep through a large changing workspace. The separate intake consumes a ground-access region that can conflict with the arm trajectory. Wiring must survive joint motion and remain replaceable. Exact package coordinates, loaded inertias, pickup mouth width and battery removal route are not established by this selected review.
independent_motions: Shoulder, elbow and wrist are three positioning coordinates. The cube intake and gripper add powered functions; their deployment and transport must be audited before giving a whole-robot DOF or motor total. High moment of inertia is an owner concern; actual loaded inertia is not measured here.
burdens_avoided: An articulated arm can reach multiple positions without forcing the chassis to follow one fixed mast line. A dedicated collector can decouple a generous ground-capture mouth from the smaller placing hand. These are potential advantages that a fixed-lift alternative must explicitly match.
burdens_retained: Multiple joint states require calibration, safe transit paths, dynamic control and recovery from interrupted motion. A handoff adds possession transfer, support and timing requirements. The wiring tradeoff shows service access and impact protection can conflict. More complexity is not proof of poor reliability; retain the team repair report as counterevidence.
engineering_hypothesis: An arm is worthwhile when its workspace and acquisition advantages save more complete-cycle time or failures than its coordination costs create. For a team whose required poses fit a fixed mast, that flexibility may be unnecessary expense. Compare reachable task sets before comparing mechanism prestige.
rival_explanation: Better control software can make extra coordinates fast and consistent, and a well-developed handoff may outperform direct narrow-mouth pickup. Alliance outcomes cannot isolate architecture from execution or partners.
reversal_conditions: Prefer articulation if the fixed mast cannot legally reach essential poses, requires slow repositioning, or loses acquisition reliability. Prefer the fixed lift when it meets the same task envelope and measured cycle targets with lower development/service burden.
unknowns: Actual inertia, comparable complete-cycle distributions, full cone route, failure recovery behavior, exact event-installed code and final mechanical configuration. Code execution was not simulated or hardware tested.
decision_changing_check: Map identical task poses, legal extensions and intake clearances. Estimate masses and arm inertias from real geometry instead of adjectives. Compare acquisition, handoff and scoring times separately, then combine them with failures; inspect interruption recovery in code before any physical trial.
outcome_status: No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

title: Compare paths and iteration costs, not intake names
version_label: BLITZ original versus RE-BLITZ rebuild; inherited physical studies

premises.text: Two collectors approach the chassis from opposite sides. They feed a constrained serpentine path and a fixed-yaw launcher rather than a deep open bulk hopper. The launcher structure occupies one end of the base, while the four-bar links occupy side deployment space. The binder base image shows four corner drive modules and a lightened pan. Electronics under the pan require turning the robot over and removing its protective belly sheet according to the team release; do not draw those electronics as accessible through the ball path. Battery removal direction is not established. A fixed launcher can aim with the chassis while the side collectors sweep laterally, but that is a control and route advantage, not unrestricted acquisition in every heading.

The rebuild uses a single front slapdown collector, an expanding storage enclosure over an inclined roller floor, and a full-width raised shooter at the opposite end. Corner swerve modules sit below this path; the launcher side structure carries the drum and hood and attaches down toward the drive rails. Source dimensions give a 27.5 by 27-inch frame. The hopper panels and their joints surround the ball path, so screw heads on the hood can rub a sliding wall. A source reply specifically explains using flathead screws there. Some electronics moved above the brainpan, but under-pan equipment still needs underside access. Preserve that service split. Do not infer battery removal without its source view.

piece_flow: Original: two collectors → constrained serpentine transport → fixed launcher. Rebuild: slapdown acquisition → bulk hopper/roller-floor path → launcher. Read both full physical studies; the original inlet merge and several rebuilt interfaces remain unknown.
packaging: The original places deployment links beside a constrained transport path. The rebuild allocates inventory volume and an active floor beneath it. Mouth deployment, stored inventory, launcher support and electronics access must be evaluated as one package; a compact intake alone says little about sustained feed.
independent_motions: Count collector deployment coordinates separately from roller motors, floor drive and hood motion. Two collectors do not automatically double throughput, and a single slapdown does not make the hopper feed problem disappear.
burdens_avoided: A less constrained bulk path can avoid repeated direction changes and dedicated conveyor transitions, if pieces can still reach the feeder consistently. Fewer deployment linkages may simplify impact recovery and replacement.
burdens_retained: Bulk inventory introduces bridging, starvation, compression and center-of-mass effects. An active floor adds contact and power demands. Rebuild development time is itself a cost; no numerical time saving or causal season improvement is established by the reviewed construction.
engineering_hypothesis: Evaluate pickup rate, usable stored capacity and sustained release together. A simple mechanism that starves the launcher cannot meet an elite throughput target. Conversely, a more elaborate collector that feeds no faster may spend space and iteration budget without useful benefit.
rival_explanation: The apparent improvement may depend on launcher changes, code, field strategy or testing maturity, rather than collector topology alone. Treat the before/after history as a source of hypotheses, not a controlled experiment.
reversal_conditions: A constrained path may win when orientation/order matters or bulk feed is unreliable. A bulk path may win when high inventory and simultaneous feed dominate. Select using the new game piece and geometry, not the historical team name.
unknowns: Common-condition rates, exact interface geometry, actual jam frequency and isolated effects of each redesign. Do not infer hidden plumbing or installed pairings from different binder snapshots.
decision_changing_check: Before replacing an architecture, calculate capacity, clearances and bottleneck rates. Test the single most uncertain transfer or hopper-floor section only if its outcome can change the decision.
outcome_status: No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.
